::: {.lead}
Today you summarize a long list in Excel, you ask it new questions, and you
test an AI summary of the numbers. Each experiment has two parts. **Part
A** is in Excel and an AI assistant on the lab computer. **Part B** is on a
simulator of the interactive lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the
screen, click its link. After each step, write your result in its box. At
the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with Excel (the desktop app, or Excel on the
  web at `office.com`) and an AI assistant that the university allows (for
  example `copilot.microsoft.com` with your university account).
- **No lab computer today?** Do Part B of each experiment on your phone. Do
  Part A later on any computer with Excel.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · A PivotTable

**The idea:** a **PivotTable** makes a **summary table** of a long list in
a few clicks. Click one cell of the list › **Insert › PivotTable** › OK.
Then drag a field to **Rows** (the groups) and a number field to
**Values** (what Excel adds up). Do not type the totals by hand: typed
numbers do not change when the list changes.

**Aim:** make a summary table of the 24 sales of March.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Open `month-start.xlsx` (click **Enable Editing** if you see it). Click
   one cell of the list. Choose **Insert › PivotTable** and click **OK**.

   {{< record "Where is the PivotTable? What is on the right?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Excel adds a **new sheet** with an empty PivotTable. The **PivotTable
   Fields** pane on the right lists the headings of the list: Week, Item,
   Type, Qty and Total (JD).
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You click **OK**. Where is the new PivotTable?

   - [x] on a new sheet, with the PivotTable Fields pane on the right

     Why: The pane lists the headings of the list.

   - [ ] under the list, on the same sheet

     Why: With OK, Excel makes a new sheet for it.

   - [ ] in a new workbook

     Why: It stays in the same file, on a new sheet.
   :::

2. In the pane, drag **Type** to **Rows** and **Total (JD)** to **Values**.

   {{< record "Paper … ; Drinks … ; Bags … ; Grand Total …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Paper 206, Drinks 71, Bags 78; Grand Total 355 JD.** One row for each
   type, and the sum of its totals. Paper sold the most.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="206" unit="JD" hint="Read the row of Paper in the PivotTable."}
   How much did **Paper** sell?

   Why: Paper 206, Drinks 71, Bags 78; Grand Total 355 JD: Paper sold the most.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-13/sims/pivot-lab.html" poster="../../week-13/sims/pivot-lab.png" title="Pivot Lab: summarize Rana's month" >}}

3. In **Pivot Lab**, choose Rows **Item** and Values **Sum of Total**.
   Which item brought the most money?

   {{< record "The item … ; its total …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Notebook, 148 JD.** The row field decides the groups: by type, by
   week or by item. The Grand Total stays 355 JD.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Rows **Item**, Values **Sum of Total**. What does each row show?

   - [x] one item, and the money of all its sales

     Why: Excel adds up the totals of each item.

   - [ ] one sale of the list

     Why: A PivotTable groups the sales; it does not copy them.

   - [ ] the number of sales of each item

     Why: That is Count of sales, not Sum of Total.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · New questions, same table

**The idea:** the same PivotTable answers new questions. Change the **row
field** (Week instead of Type) or the calculation (**Value Field Settings
› Average**). **PivotTable Analyze › PivotChart › Line** makes a **line
chart** of the weeks. A PivotTable does not change by itself: after a
change in the list, click **PivotTable Analyze › Refresh**.

**Aim:** ask new questions to the same table, and keep it up to date.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Drag **Type** out of Rows, and drag **Week** into Rows. Then click a
   cell of the PivotTable and choose **PivotTable Analyze › PivotChart ›
   Line** › OK.

   {{< record "Weeks 1 to 4: … ; the best … ; the weakest …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **87, 63, 112 and 93 JD.** The **third** week was the best, and the
   **second** the weakest. The line goes down from week 1 to week 2 and
   from week 3 to week 4. The Grand Total stays 355 JD.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   Put the weeks of March in order, from the best to the weakest.

   1. week 3: 112 JD
   2. week 4: 93 JD
   3. week 1: 87 JD
   4. week 2: 63 JD

   Why: The third week was the best, and the second the weakest.
   :::

2. Go to the sheet **March**. Change the total of the bag in week 3 from
   **48** to **58**. Look at week 3 in the PivotTable. Then choose
   **PivotTable Analyze › Refresh**.

   {{< record "Week 3 before Refresh … ; after Refresh …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **112** before Refresh, **122** after. A PivotTable does not change by
   itself. Now change 58 back to **48** and refresh again.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="122" unit="JD" hint="The bag in week 3 is now 10 JD more."}
   The bag of week 3 is now 58 JD. What does week 3 show **after** Refresh?

   Why: 112 + 10 = 122 JD. Before Refresh it still shows 112.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-13/sims/pivot-lab.html" poster="../../week-13/sims/pivot-lab.png" title="Pivot Lab: summarize Rana's month" >}}

3. In **Pivot Lab**, choose Rows **Type** and Values **Average of Total**.
   Which type has the biggest average sale?

   {{< record "Average sale: Paper … ; Drinks … ; Bags …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Paper 20.6, Drinks 7.1, Bags 19.5 JD.** Paper has the biggest average
   sale. The same list answers a new question.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   With **Average**, which type has the biggest average sale?

   - [x] Paper, 20.6 JD

     Why: Paper 20.6, Bags 19.5 and Drinks 7.1 JD.

   - [ ] Bags, 19.5 JD

     Why: Close, but 19.5 is less than 20.6.

   - [ ] Drinks, 7.1 JD

     Why: The smallest average.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · An AI summary

**The idea:** an AI tool can describe the numbers fast, but a sentence can
sound sure and still be wrong: an AI can even invent a number (a
**hallucination**). Give it only the **summary table**, with no personal
data. Ask for three short sentences, each with a number, and check every
number with the PivotTable. A **data insight** is a short, true sentence
such as "Paper sold the most". Add an **AI-use statement** under the text.

**Aim:** let an AI tool describe the numbers, then check every number.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the apps (Excel and an AI assistant)**
:::

1. Put **Type** in Rows again, with Values **Sum of Total (JD)**. Select
   the PivotTable and copy it. In the AI assistant, type *Write three short
   sentences about these sales of March, each with a number:* and paste the
   table.

   {{< record "Numbers that are right … ; wrong or invented …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Check each number with the table: Paper **206**, Drinks **71**, Bags
   **78**, total **355** JD. Check a share with a calculator (Paper: 206 ÷
   355 ≈ 58 %). Delete or correct every wrong or invented number.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   An AI wrote four sentences about March. Check each number with the
   table: Paper 206, Drinks 71, Bags 78, total 355 JD.

   Right: keep it
   :   The total of March was 355 JD.

       Why: The Grand Total is 355 JD.

   :   Paper made about 58 % of the sales.

       Why: 206 ÷ 355 ≈ 0.58, so about 58 %.

   Wrong: correct or delete it
   :   Drinks sold 91 JD.

       Why: The table says 71 JD.

   :   The sales of March were 400 JD.

       Why: The Grand Total is 355 JD.
   :::

2. Under the PivotTable, write your own summary: three true sentences,
   each with a number, and one sentence of AI-use statement.

   {{< record "My best sentence, and my AI-use statement" lines=3 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good summary: "March sales were 355 JD. Paper sold the most, 206 JD.
   The best week was the third, with 112 JD." A good statement: "I used
   Copilot for a first draft and checked every number with the
   PivotTable."
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which summary is good?

   - [x] March sales were 355 JD. Paper sold the most, 206 JD. The best week was the third, with 112 JD.

     Why: Three true sentences, each with a number from the PivotTable.

   - [ ] Sales were very good. Everybody worked hard.

     Why: No numbers to check, and no facts.

   - [ ] March sales were 355 JD. Bags sold the most.

     Why: Paper sold the most (206 JD), not Bags.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-13/sims/summary-check.html" poster="../../week-13/sims/summary-check.png" title="Summary Check: is the AI right?" >}}

3. In **Summary Check**, mark each of the six AI sentences true or wrong.
   Which sentences are wrong?

   {{< record "The wrong sentences" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Wrong:** "Bags sold the most" (Paper did, 206 JD); "Sales grew every
   week" (the second week fell); "The biggest single sale was a bag for 48
   JD" (the notebooks, 60 JD). The other three are true.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   True or wrong? Sort the sentences of Summary Check.

   True
   :   Total sales in March were 355 JD.

       Why: The Grand Total is 355 JD.

   :   The third week was the best, with 112 JD.

       Why: 112 JD is the highest week.

   Wrong
   :   Bags sold the most, because each bag is expensive.

       Why: Paper sold the most (206 JD); Bags only 78 JD.

   :   Sales grew every week.

       Why: The second week (63 JD) was lower than the first (87 JD).
   :::

## Game challenge · Huda's April meeting

Finished early? In April the Sunrise shop sold **400 JD**: **Paper 180
JD**, **Drinks 95 JD** and **Bags 125 JD**; the four weeks had **90, 110,
85 and 115 JD**. An AI tool writes: "Drinks sold the most. The best week
was the fourth, with 115 JD. Sales fell in the third week." Which sentence
is wrong? Then check your answers in **Try it 4** of the interactive
lesson.
